description_full: RBC Bearings Incorporated manufactures and markets engineered precision bearings, components, and systems in the United States and internationally. It operates through two segments: Aerospace/Defense and Industrial. The company produces plain bearings with self-lubricating or metal-to-metal designs, including rod end bearings, spherical plain bearings, and journal bearings; roller bearings, such as tapered roller bearings, needle roller bearings, and needle bearing track rollers and cam followers, which are anti-friction products that are used in industrial applications and military aircraft platforms; and ball bearings that include high precision aerospace, airframe control, thin section, and industrial ball bearings that utilize high precision ball elements to reduce friction in high-speed applications. In addition, it offers mounted bearing products include mounted ball bearings, mounted roller bearings, and mounted plain bearings; and enclosed gearing product lines, including quantis gearmotor, torque arm, tigear, magnagear and maxum, and controlled start transmission. Further, the company's power transmission components include mechanical drive components, couplings, and conveyor components; engineered hydraulics and valves for aircraft and submarine applications, and aerospace and defense aftermarket services; fasteners; precision mechanical components, for use in various general industrial applications; and machine tool collets that are used for holding circulars or rod-like pieces. It serves commercial and defense aerospace, construction, mining, forestry, energy, agricultural, food and beverage, metals and mining material handling, chemicals, oil and gas production, warehousing and logistics, semiconductor equipment, waste and water management, and rail and transportation applications through its direct sales force, and a network of industrial and aerospace distributors. The company was founded in 1919 and is based in Oxford, Connecticut.

financial_summary: RBC Bearings Incorporated is a large-cap industrials business with a $15.0B market cap on $1.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years and +12% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 7% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 38%.

The business throws off $343M in free cash flow — roughly 18 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.45× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 8.5×.

Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 19% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 18% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 29% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 29% and a beta of 1.00, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $139.0M traded a day, and interest is running hot at 1.6x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 55% in the 2020 crash, 26% in the 2022 bear market and 71% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $217 (margin of safety -119%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 25%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $140 to $339 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 42.4 vs 23.3, EV/EBITDA 24.3 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 43.8 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 3% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 9 covering analysts target $609 on average, 28% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 7% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.4%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.36).
It runs a 38% gross margin and converts 18% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.45x.
ROE of 9% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.8% of revenue on R&D and 1.8% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.5x net debt to EBITDA ($57.3M of cash against $875.5M of debt), with interest covered 8.5x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 6.4, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 282 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
Goodwill makes up 39% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.4% over 3 years, 25.2% over 5 years and 12.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 19%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 19.5% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.39 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 68% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 210%.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (3.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 42, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.6%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
The share count has grown 6.0% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 5,816 employees, each generates about $322K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 11.3% a year.
That works out to $59K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.8M (15x revenue per employee).
